title: The Valuation Habit Most Owners Skip Until They're Already Trying to Sell
excerpt: Most Australian SME owners get a real number on their business exactly once, the week they decide to sell. By then there is no runway left to act on what it reveals.
content:
Australian Small Business Month tends to produce the same ritual every October. Owners tidy the sales pipeline, review staffing before the run into Christmas, and dust off a budget spreadsheet that has not been opened since July. Almost nobody uses the month to ask the one question that actually compounds over a ten year horizon: what is this business worth right now, with no deal on the table and nobody asking?

For most owner-led businesses, the first time a real number gets put on the business is the week a sale process starts, a bank asks for a valuation to support a lending decision, or a departing co-director forces the question. The valuation lands correctly in every one of those cases. It is just arriving too late to be useful for anything beyond settling a figure that is already in motion.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses is that a valuation commissioned on an ordinary Tuesday, with no sale anywhere in sight, behaves differently. It stops being a verdict and starts being a diagnostic, showing plainly which parts of the business carry real value and which parts only look like they do from behind the owner's desk.

What the Number Often Shows That the Calendar Does Not

A business can be trading well by every measure an owner watches week to week, a full diary, steady revenue, a comfortable bank balance, and still come back from a valuation lower than expected. The methodology behind an EBITDA multiple, discounted cash flow or asset-based approach is not interested in how busy the business feels. It is interested in how much of the earnings would survive the owner stepping back, how concentrated the revenue is across customers, and how defensible the margin looks without the founder's personal relationships propping it up.

Owners often arrive with a number already in their head, usually anchored to a multiple of revenue overheard at an industry event or attached to a competitor's rumoured sale price. That guess is rarely close, because a revenue multiple ignores the one variable that actually decides price, which is how much of that revenue converts into earnings a new owner could actually rely on without the founder in the room.

These gaps are not failures. They are the pattern across almost every owner-led SME that has grown on relationships and personal reputation rather than systems, because that is how most good businesses actually start. The valuation simply makes visible what day to day trading never has reason to show. An indicative business valuation exists for exactly this moment, well before anyone has decided to sell, while there is still time to act on what it finds.

Why Timing Changes What You Can Actually Do With the Number

Customer concentration takes the better part of a year to diversify properly. Reducing owner dependence, building a second layer of management that a buyer or a bank will actually trust, takes longer again, and it often overlaps with the same readiness work covered in an exit readiness review. None of that can start the week a sale process does, because by then the business is being presented, not rebuilt. Get the same number eighteen months earlier and it stops being a post-mortem. It becomes a list, ranked by dollar impact, of exactly what to fix first, with enough runway to actually work through it before anyone outside the business is asking questions.

A Spring Number, Not a Sale Decision

October sits in a useful pocket of the calendar. The EOFY figures have settled, the numbers are clean, and Christmas trading pressure is still a few months off. It is a sensible point in the year to treat a valuation the way a board treats an annual budget, a fixed check-in rather than something only done under pressure. Owners who know their number, and understand which three levers would actually move it, tend to make calmer decisions about staffing, pricing and reinvestment than owners who are guessing, because they are weighing those decisions against a real figure rather than a hopeful one.

None of this requires a decision to sell. It requires roughly two weeks, a clean set of financials, and the willingness to hear a number that might not match the one in your head. For owners who want that starting point, or who already have a number and want to know what would move it, a discovery call is the easiest place to begin.

faqs.q: How often should an Australian SME get a business valuation done?
faqs.a: There is no fixed rule, but many owner-led businesses benefit from a fresh number every two to three years, or sooner after a significant change in revenue, staffing or ownership. An indicative business valuation is usually enough to track direction without the cost of a full formal report.

faqs.q: Does getting a valuation mean I am planning to sell my business?
faqs.a: No. Most owners who commission a valuation outside of a live sale process are doing it for clarity, not because a transaction is imminent. It is common to use the number for succession planning, partner buy-ins, bank conversations or simply to understand where the business actually stands today.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an indicative and a full formal business valuation?
faqs.a: An indicative valuation gives a defensible range using the same core methods a buyer would apply, which is useful for planning and benchmarking. A more detailed formal valuation meets the standard required for a sale negotiation, shareholder dispute or capital raise, and carries more weight with a third party.

faqs.q: What do business buyers notice that an owner often misses day to day?
faqs.a: Buyers weigh customer concentration, how dependent the business is on the owner personally, and the quality behind the revenue line, not just its size. These are the same dimensions covered in an exit readiness review, and they rarely show up in the numbers an owner checks week to week.

faqs.q: How long does it take to lift a low valuation once you know what is holding it back?
faqs.a: It depends on the driver. Diversifying a concentrated customer base or building a management layer that reduces owner dependence typically takes twelve to eighteen months of deliberate work. That is exactly why the earlier the number is known, the more of that runway is actually available to use.

faqs.q: Is a business valuation useful for reasons other than selling the business?
faqs.a: Yes. Lenders, incoming partners and family members stepping into the business all tend to ask the same underlying question in different words, which is what the business is actually worth. Having a current, defensible number on hand removes a layer of friction from each of those conversations, and is worth having before anyone asks, not after.
